name: Massage / foam rolling / recovery gear

lead: Foam rolling means rolling a muscle over a foam cylinder using body weight, a practice called self-myofascial release. People use it with other massage tools to feel less sore and more flexible, so they can train more often and keep posture and movement in good shape.

Body weight presses the muscle against the roller. Researchers have reported short-term increases in joint range of motion, with long-term effects unknown, and post-exercise rolling has been reported to reduce perceived muscle pain. Reviews describe the evidence as favouring use as a warm-up more than as a recovery tool. Appearance outcomes have not been studied.

paras: People roll major muscle groups before training as a warm-up or afterward for soreness, usually for a minute or so per area. Massage guns and balls are used the same way. It is commonly combined with stretching and mobility work.
The sources reviewed do not describe specific risks. Bruising or pain can occur with heavy pressure, and people with circulation problems or injuries are generally advised to ask a clinician.

angle.text: Foam rollers and massage tools ease soreness and loosen tight muscles so you can train more often and move better, supporting physique and posture. Studies report short-term gains in range of motion; appearance has not been studied.

lead: Foam rollers are lightweight cylinders of elastomeric foam that a person places between a muscle and the floor and rolls over using body weight, a practice classed as self-myofascial release.[1] Proponents use them, along with related massage tools, to increase flexibility, reduce soreness and ease muscle knots.[1]

In posture and body-recovery discussions, such tools are grouped as recovery gear. Published research summarized on Wikipedia reports a short-term improvement in joint range of motion, unknown long-term effects, and a view that the evidence better supports foam rolling as a warm-up activity than as a recovery tool, although post-exercise rolling has been reported to reduce perceived muscle pain.[1]

paras: A foam roller is used by lying or leaning on it so that body weight presses a muscle against the cylinder, which is then rolled back and forth. Firmness ranges from soft to firm, and softer versions are generally suggested for beginners.[1]

A 2015 review by Cheatham and colleagues found a short-term positive effect on joint range of motion, while a 2019 review by Hughes and Ramer concluded that long-term benefits are unknown.[1] A 2021 analysis by Konrad and colleagues found no significant range-of-motion difference between combining rolling with stretching and doing either alone.[1]

A meta-analysis by Wiewelhove and colleagues concluded that the evidence appears to justify foam rolling mainly as a warm-up activity rather than a recovery tool, while also reporting reduced muscle pain perception after post-exercise rolling.[1] Hughes and Ramer suggested that roughly 90 seconds per muscle group may be the minimum for a short-term reduction in soreness, but noted insufficient evidence on the optimal amount.[1]

Delayed onset muscle soreness typically peaks 24 to 72 hours after unaccustomed exercise and usually resolves within about a week.[2] Measures that increase blood flow, including massage, are described as possibly helping somewhat, but the article does not provide detailed evidence on massage.[2]
Human trials of foam rolling exist for range of motion, warm-up and soreness outcomes, as summarized above.[1] No studies found specific to appearance or posture outcomes in looksmaxxing contexts.
